statement: What makes body temperature rise more after MDMA is not settled. This claim rests on one narrative review (Parrott, 2012) of small studies, so its figures are second-hand and given as summarized by the review. In placebo-controlled laboratory studies of 4 to 16 volunteers each, the review puts the average peak rise in core temperature at +0.1 degrees Celsius at doses up to 1.0 mg/kg, +0.4 at 1.1 to 1.9 mg/kg and +0.7 at 2.0 mg/kg, from studies using different body sites; in the one study of 8 men that gave 75 mg and 125 mg, the peak was +0.4 at both. In two small studies at 2.0 mg/kg in rooms at 18 and 30 degrees, the rise was +1.0 and +0.8 in 4 volunteers and +0.4 and +0.6 in 10, which the review describes as nearly identical or broadly similar in the two rooms, although its own table of factors lists a high room temperature as associated with a higher core temperature. The rise differs between people: in 8 volunteers the group average was +0.4 but one person peaked at +1.9; at a dance party the two people with the highest MDMA blood levels (0.77 and 0.84 mg/l) had the largest rises (+1.0 and +1.6), while across 27 people the link between blood level and rise was borderline (r = +0.38, p = 0.058) and there was no night without MDMA to compare. In studies at dance clubs and parties, of 11 to 41 people each and with different comparisons, group peak rises ranged from +0.2 to +1.6 degrees (+1.8 on the skin in one), the largest in 11 people who took 6 tablets on average over a night; the review reports no comparison within them of amounts, dancing, room heat or crowding. It says data on dancing and on other drugs are very limited, that crowding and loud music have not been investigated, and that hydration, age, sex, genes and personality need to be investigated in people. Overheating to 40 degrees and above, some of it fatal, is known from hospital case reports, which cannot show how often it happens; in a UK report of 7 deaths and 4 further cases of this kind, plasma MDMA ranged from 0.11 to 1.26 mg/l, which its authors said did not reflect high doses, and in another case a friend who took the same MDMA had no thermal reaction. How hot people feel also differs: in an Internet survey of over 200 people who take ecstasy, 16 in 100 did not feel hot, 41 slightly, 31 moderately and 12 strongly or extremely, and the review offers as a hypothesis for future study that people with low thermal awareness might be most at risk. Some people feel little from an amount and take more; the review notes continuous dancing and bingeing for over 48 hours without sleep in experienced people with greater tolerance, and calls the effects of that currently unknown. In 166 volunteers resting at about 22.7 degrees (a pooled laboratory analysis), 125 mg raised the average highest ear temperature by 0.3 degrees (37.7 against 37.4) and 24 in 100 crossed 38 degrees against 9 in 100 on placebo; the test of a dose effect between 75 and 125 mg was not significant. Those volunteers rested, took one pure dose and were not dancing, crowded or on other drugs, so the laboratory studies cannot show what heat, dancing, crowding, other drugs or more MDMA do to temperature, and the party studies cannot separate them either.
plain: Nobody can yet say what makes some people get hotter than others with MDMA. In small lab studies of people at rest, body temperature rose by about 0.4 degrees on average at moderate doses and 0.7 at higher ones, and by 1.9 in one person. At dance parties the average rise ran from 0.2 to 1.6 degrees, but the studies compared different things, so heat, dancing, crowds, other drugs and extra tablets cannot be told apart. Overheating to 40 degrees or more is known from hospital case reports, which cannot show how often it happens. Not everyone feels hot: in one survey 16 in 100 did not. Some people feel little from an amount and take more; what that does to temperature has not been studied. This comes from one review of small studies, so the numbers are second-hand.
population: People given MDMA in placebo-controlled laboratory studies (4 to 16 volunteers each), people studied at dance clubs and house parties (11 to 41 each), and people treated in hospital for severe overheating (case reports and series), all as summarized in one narrative review; the 166 volunteers of one pooled laboratory analysis read in full as a qualifier
exposure: MDMA, by dose in the laboratory (study conditions: up to 1.0, 1.1 to 1.9 and 2.0 mg/kg; 75 and 125 mg) and by tablets taken over a night in party studies (1 to 6 tablets, other drugs sometimes taken); room temperature (18 and 30 degrees Celsius in two studies), dancing, crowding, other drugs and hydration as possible modifiers
comparator: Placebo in laboratory studies; an abstinent weekend, people not taking ecstasy at the same club, the evening before, or no comparison in the party studies
outcome: Peak rise in core temperature (rectal, swallowed sensor, ear, mouth or armpit), in degrees Celsius; severe overheating (40 degrees Celsius and above)
magnitude: Laboratory, peak change in core temperature, average across the studies in the review's table: +0.1 degrees Celsius (doses up to 1.0 mg/kg), +0.4 (1.1 to 1.9 mg/kg), +0.7 (2.0 mg/kg); different body sites, 4 to 16 volunteers per study, no intervals. In one study, 75 mg and 125 mg both +0.4 (8 men). Rooms at 18 and 30 degrees: +1.0 and +0.8 (4 volunteers) and +0.4 and +0.6 (10 volunteers). One study of 8 volunteers: group mean +0.4, highest individual +1.9. Dance clubs and parties, group peak change: +0.2 (27 people), +1.2 (32), +0.3 (12), +1.6 (11, 6 tablets on average), +1.1 oral and +1.8 skin (41); comparisons differ. One party study: blood level against rise r = +0.38, p = 0.058 (27 people). Internet survey of over 200 people: did not feel hot 16%, slightly 41%, moderately 31%, strongly or extremely 12%. Severe overheating (40 to 43 degrees): case reports and series only, no denominator. Laboratory study read in full, 125 mg against placebo (136 people): average highest ear temperature 37.7 against 37.4, above 38 degrees in 24% against 9%.

evidence.locator: Section 2 > Body temperature in laboratory studies, paragraphs on Tancer et al. (2003) (starting p. 2, right column) and Freedman et al. (2005) (p. 3, left column)
evidence.extracted: As summarized by the review: 4 volunteers (Tancer and colleagues) and 10 volunteers (Freedman and colleagues) were given 2.0 mg/kg and placebo in rooms at 18 and at 30 degrees Celsius. Core temperature rose +1.0 and +0.8 degrees in the cool and warm rooms in the first study (rectal probes) and +0.4 and +0.6 in the second (swallowed sensor); the review says core temperature values were nearly identical in the two rooms in the first study and that the effects of MDMA were broadly similar under both room conditions in the second. In the second study the onset of sweating was delayed.

evidence.locator: Section 2, paragraph on Kolbrich et al. (2008) (starts p. 3, right column, continues p. 4, left column); Section 3 > Body temperature in dance club studies, 1st paragraph on Irvine et al. (2006) (p. 4, left column)
evidence.extracted: As summarized by the review: in 8 volunteers given 1.0 and 1.6 mg/kg (Kolbrich and colleagues) the ear-temperature rise (+0.3 and +0.4 degrees Celsius against placebo) was not significant, but the link between blood MDMA and temperature rise was (p < 0.0001). At a dance party, 27 people (Irvine and colleagues) were measured the evening before, at 4 am and at 10 am: the rise was about +0.2 and not significant, there was no control night so the fall of body temperature during the night was not accounted for, 5 people had particularly high blood MDMA, and the two people with the highest levels (0.77 and 0.84 mg/l) had the largest individual rises (+1.0 and +1.6 degrees); across the group the link between blood level and rise was borderline (r = +0.38, p = 0.058). Methamphetamine and cannabis were present in 41% and 33% of the group.

evidence.locator: Table 2 (p. 3, right column); Section 3 > Body temperature in dance club studies, paragraphs on Parrott and Young (2005), Parrott et al. (2008) and the third study (Parrott et al., 2007b) (p. 4, right column)
evidence.extracted: Group peak change in temperature at dance clubs and parties, as summarized by the review, with different comparisons: +0.2 degrees Celsius (27 people, no control night); +1.2 (32 people who had taken ecstasy that evening, against 26 controls at the same club who had not); +0.3 (12 people, ecstasy weekend against an abstinent weekend; the difference borderline, p = 0.08); +1.6 (11 people who took 6 tablets on average over a night, at house parties); +1.1 oral and +1.8 skin (41 people, Morefield and colleagues). Table 2 notes that the control conditions and procedures for statistical analysis varied across studies.

evidence.locator: Section 3, paragraph on Morefield et al. (2009) (starts p. 4, right column, ends p. 5, left column); Section 4 > Clinical hyperthermia and its treatment, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 5)
evidence.extracted: As summarized by the review: 41 people at dance parties in Australia took 1 to 5 tablets, 25% had blood levels in the toxic to lethal range by forensic guidelines, and the authors said these high doses were generally well tolerated. Severe overheating is known from case reports and series, with no denominator: 41.6 degrees Celsius 2 hours after 100 to 150 mg of MDMA powder in a woman whose friend took the same MDMA without a thermal reaction; a 16-year-old who took one tablet, her second time, had 0.424 mg/l MDMA and died after 36 hours; a UK poisons-unit report of 7 deaths with admission temperatures of 40 to 43 degrees and 4 further severe cases, in which plasma MDMA ranged from 0.11 to 1.26 mg/l and the authors said the severe reactions did not reflect high dose levels.

evidence.locator: Table 3 (factors associated with the thermal effects of ecstasy/MDMA): rows on dance clubs, crowding, polydrug aspects, ambient temperature and other factors (p. 4)
evidence.extracted: The review's own table of factors: for dancing, the data are very limited; for crowding and loud music, effects have not been empirically investigated; for stimulant and sedative co-drugs, empirical data are very limited; for age, sex, genes, hydration and personality, they need to be empirically investigated; for the room, a laboratory row says high ambient temperature was associated with higher core temperature with complex combined effects. Dose and plasma level are listed with laboratory support (p < 0.0001 for plasma level) and, in a party study, a borderline correlation (p = 0.058). Editors' note: the text on p. 3 describes the effects as broadly similar at 18 and 30 degrees Celsius.

evidence.locator: Section 5 > Thermal self-ratings, 2nd paragraph (p. 6, left column)
evidence.extracted: As summarized by the review: in an Internet survey of over 200 people who take ecstasy (Parrott and colleagues, 2006), 16% said they did not feel hot when on MDMA, 41% felt slightly hot, 31% moderately hot and 12% strongly or extremely hot, which the review takes as showing wide variation in how hot people feel.

evidence.locator: Section 7 > Behavioural and environmental co-stressors, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 7, left column into right column); Section 8 > Overview, 1st paragraph (p. 7, right column)
evidence.extracted: The review says some people dance continuously and binge on MDMA for more than 48 hours without sleep, especially experienced people with greater tolerance, and that the effects of these periods are currently unknown. It lists as factors that would increase thermal stress higher single doses or successive binge doses, prolonged dancing, and crowded clubs with high ambient temperatures (citing surveys and observations), and says hydration needs to be investigated in people. It puts forward as a hypothesis for future study that people with low thermal awareness might be most at risk. In the Overview, in 8 volunteers given 1.6 mg/kg (Kolbrich and colleagues) the group mean rise was +0.4 degrees Celsius but one volunteer peaked at +1.9.
evidence.quote: those with low thermal awareness might be most at risk from developing severe hyperthermia

evidence.locator: Table 2, 125 mg block (n = 136), temperature rows, and the Drug x dose columns (p. 582)
evidence.extracted: In the laboratory at rest, 125 mg of MDMA raised the average highest ear temperature from 37.4 (SD 0.5) on placebo to 37.7 (SD 0.5); 32 of 136 people (24%) went above 38 degrees on MDMA and 12 (9%) on placebo; the highest value was 39.1 against 38.7. The test of a dose effect on temperature between 75 and 125 mg (different people in different studies) was not significant (F 2.43).

Temperatures did not rise above 39.1 degrees Celsius. The authors call a temperature above 40 rare and the most important life-threatening complication of recreational MDMA use, say no controlled clinical study has reported it, and suggest this may be because participants had moderate single doses at rest, were well hydrated and were not in a hot or crowded place.

risk_of_bias.note: The review's methods are a personal collection of papers plus a PubMed search, and it cannot be appraised for bias (narrative review; high on the card on the editors' five-domain checklist). Its party studies lack comparable controls: no control night in one, a different comparison group in each of the others.

inconsistency.note: Party-study peaks run from +0.2 to +1.6 degrees Celsius with different comparisons and no explanation; the review's table says a warm room goes with a higher core temperature while its text says the effects were broadly similar.

indirectness.note: Second-hand through one review; most primary studies are not in the library. Laboratory studies at rest do not bear on dancing, crowding or heat, and party studies do not separate them.

imprecision.note: Samples of 4 to 41 people, no intervals; the large individual differences (+1.9 in one of 8) show that group means hide the spread.

grade.reasoning: A claim seen only through a narrative review starts from the design of the primary studies the review describes (small placebo-controlled laboratory studies, uncontrolled party studies, case reports) and is downgraded for risk of bias and indirectness (METHODS 6.3). Observational start (low); down four levels in all (risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision), bounded at very low. Relation: evidence is insufficient to say whether dose, heat, dancing, crowding, other drugs or hydration change the rise, because no study separates them and the review says so itself. Status mixed: party studies disagree in size without an explanation, and the review's table and text disagree about room temperature. Draft: the claim rests only on a narrative review (METHODS 6.3); the pooled laboratory analysis read in full is a qualifying anchor, and the single quotation is the review's hypothesis, which it marks as untested.

verification.flag_note: Review-only claim. The primary papers (Grob 1996, Vollenweider 1998, Mas 1999, Tancer 2003, Freedman 2005, Irvine 2006, Parrott and Young 2005, Parrott 2007b and 2008, Kolbrich 2008, Morefield 2009, Henry 1992, Chadwick 1991, Brown and Osterloh 1987, Patel 2005) have no reference record here and were not read; their numbers are the review's. The review's Table 1 'overall mean' rows average studies that used different body sites and different dose units, and Table 2's comparisons differ by study. The review's Table 3 says a high room temperature goes with a higher core temperature; its text (p. 3) says the effects were broadly similar at 18 and 30 degrees.
